papers.title: Meditation Depth Enhances the Functional Signal-to-Noise Ratio of the Brain
papers.abstract: Across contemplative traditions, deeper states of meditation are described as states of heightened clarity, vividness, and stillness of mind, yet what this clarity corresponds to in the brain has remained difficult to specify. The functional signal-to-noise ratio (f-SNR) framework frames mental clarity as a measurable property of neural signals: the degree to which brain activity tracks the causes of sensory signals rather than task-irrelevant endogenous activity. It predicts that deepening meditation should raise f-SNR, expressing sensory events more faithfully in neural signals against ongoing background activity. We tested this prediction across different levels of meditative depth. Twenty-nine experienced Vipassana practitioners meditated while auditory tones were presented, periodically reporting their depth of meditation. f-SNR was quantified from event-related potentials (ERPs) in a fronto-central P3 window and from single-trial decodability of auditory tone-evoked activity against no-tone background EEG. High-depth states were associated with greater ERP signal-to-noise ratio, stronger single-trial signal consistency, and improved decodability of sound tones. These results suggest that meditative depth is expressed in the reproducibility and stimulus-background separability of sensory responses, consistent with deep meditation enhancing the brain’s functional signal-to-noise ratio by improving the clarity of sensory signals and reducing task-irrelevant endogenous processes.

papers.title: Trait mindfulness and psychological distress in college students: indirect associations via experiential avoidance.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This cross-sectional study examined whether the associations between trait mindfulness and psychological distress were consistent with indirect associations involving experiential avoidance (EA) among college students. PARTICIPANTS: The sample consisted of 289 undergraduate students ( METHODS: Participants completed the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire, Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II, Multidimensional Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire, and Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. Indirect effect models were estimated with bootstrapped confidence intervals. RESULTS: Higher trait mindfulness was associated with lower EA, and higher EA was associated with greater depression, anxiety, and stress. Bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for indirect effect estimates did not include zero across outcomes and EA measures, and direct associations between mindfulness and distress remained. CONCLUSIONS: These findings are consistent with psychological flexibility theory and suggest that EA is a relevant correlate of mindfulness-distress associations in college students. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to test temporal precedence and causal mechanisms.

papers.title: The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation.
papers.abstract: A century-old tradition characterizes aesthetic experiences as intense contemplative moments in which we suspend practical concerns and devote our full attention to the object at hand. In line with this tradition, recent theories suggest that aesthetic experiences involve heightened sensory processing accompanied by a suppression of motor activity. Yet, while the link between aesthetic appreciation and perceptual enhancement has received considerable attention, the role of motor inhibition remains largely unexplored. The present study addressed this gap by investigating whether the aesthetic appreciation of images can modulate behavioral and electrophysiological markers of motor inhibition. In Experiment 1, significantly slower reaction times following the observation of preferred images were found. In Experiment 2, EEG responses associated with motor preparation and execution were significantly reduced in trials involving preferred compared with non-preferred images. Time-frequency analysis revealed significantly decreased alpha power (associated with attentional engagement toward visual perception) and increased beta power (associated with inhibited motor preparation) for preferred than non-preferred images. Overall, our results provide new evidence for the existence of a relationship between aesthetic appreciation and motor inhibition and position aesthetic experience as a valuable case study for exploring the adaptive coordination of sensory and motor systems in response to environmental demands.

papers.title: Risks of Burnout Among Mobile Crisis Team Workers in a Southern U.S. State: A Pilot Study of Work Climate and Mindfulness.
papers.abstract: The present pilot study examined burnout symptoms among frontline mental health workers in Mobile Crisis Teams (MCTs) and explored their associations with perceived work climate (an indicator of organizational resources) and individual mindfulness (an indicator of personal resources) after controlling for sex, race, and work experience, based on the Job Demands-Resources model. Survey data were collected from 50 participants offering mobile crisis services across 11 community mental health centers in a southern U.S. state, representing the full set of centers that had received funding to provide mobile crisis services statewide. Findings showed that 31.3% and 14.6% of participants disclosed moderate to high degrees of exhaustion and depersonalization - two key burnout symptoms. Also, the results of regression analyses indicated that individual mindfulness and work climate specifically helped predict participants' exhaustion and depersonalization, respectively, after controlling for sex, race, and work experience. Implications were discussed for burnout prevention among workers in MCTs.

papers.title: Perception of Special Needs Dentistry Amongst Allied Dental Professionals in Australia.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: In Australia, Dental Therapists (DTs), Dental Hygienists (DHs) and Oral Health Therapists (OHTs) encounter Special Needs (SN) patients in their clinical practice. This study investigates their perception, training, working experience and referral patterns within Special Needs Dentistry (SND). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Paper-based questionnaire was distributed to a systematically selected sample of 1000 registered DHs, DTs and OHTs who were members of professional bodies in Australia. Respondents were included irrespective of age, gender, length of working experience and country of graduation. Data analysis consisted of Chi-squared regression analysis (p < 0.05) using IBM SPSS Windows Version 29.0 (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia). RESULTS: A response rate of 49.8% (215 DTs, 107 DHs and 163 OHTs) was obtained. A significantly larger proportion of OHTs (59.5%) was aware of SND as a specialty compared to DHs (45%) and DTs (41.9%) (p < 0.05) and hence OHTs referred to SND specialists more often than other groups. In addition, 73.6% of OHTs, 63.6% of DHs and 40% of DTs had both didactic and clinical training in SND (p < 0.05). All the categories stated lack of training and continuing professional development (CPD) in SND as the main reasons for not treating SN patients. They therefore expressed interest in attending related CPD training (OHTs: 90.2%, DHs: 88.8% and DTs: 88.3%). CONCLUSIONS: OHTs demonstrated greater awareness, training, working experience and referral in SND than DHs and DTs; however, training gaps across all groups highlight the need for strengthened undergraduate education and accessible CPD in SND. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Understanding the perception of allied dental professionals regarding SND is crucial for improving access to and the quality of care for patients with special needs. Prior research has highlighted gaps in training and confidence levels amongst general practitioners; however, little is known about the perspectives of allied professionals. This study provides valuable insights into their awareness, perceived roles and educational needs, emphasizing the importance of inclusive team-based care.

papers.title: Unsupervised functional stage detection from EEG using topological data analysis.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) segmentation is still largely performed manually by specialists. Recent studies have proposed the state-detecting algorithm (SDA) - an automated technique for detecting functional stages with minimal human intervention - which has proven effective using spectral features. This paper introduces an alternative feature engineering approach that explores the spatial structure of data using the emerging field of topological data analysis (TDA). We propose an algorithm to extract a comprehensive topological description of EEG with tens of thousands of features and introduce the quick state-detecting algorithm (QSDA), a feature selection framework based on SDA performance. Next, we apply the procedure to EEG recordings from two distinct domains - Guhyasamaja Tantra meditation and whole-night polysomnographic sleep - and observe well-separated stage boundaries across most recordings, suggesting that TDA may complement or outperform spectral features in some settings. We also observed encouraging performance on noisy data, whereas shuffled epochs produced substantially weaker boundaries, supporting the robustness of the technique within the settings examined. Overall, the algorithm appears to be a promising feature engineering approach for SDA and suggests that the spatial structure of EEG may contain informative patterns. These findings motivate further investigation of their possible physiological interpretation, as well as an assessment across broader EEG paradigms.
